24 rows read. Or 1.

Without an index, a lookup reads rows one after another until it finds the match - a sequential scan.

An index is a sorted structure the database can descend, so it lands on the row instead of walking to it.

Run EXPLAIN on the query. If it says Seq Scan on a table you filter often, that is the fix.

Comment EXPLAIN and I'll send the snippet.

captions.instagram:
12 scroll events. 1 handler call.

Every scroll, resize and keystroke fires far more often than your handler needs to run.

debounce restarts a timer on each event and only runs the callback once the events stop.

The whole trick is the clearTimeout: each call cancels the pending one.

Comment DEBOUNCE and I'll send the snippet.

captions.instagram:
8 rows. 9 queries. Every request.

One query fetches the list, then the loop fires another query per row to fetch what it references.

That is the N+1: it looks like clean code and it scales linearly in round trips.

Ask for the related rows in the first query instead and the whole loop collapses into one trip.

Comment NPLUS1 and I'll send the snippet.

captions.instagram:
50 requests. 100 selects on the same table.

Your auth middleware reads the users row to check whether the account is suspended. It caches it. Then the next helper down the chain selects the same row again, microseconds later, because it has no idea the first one already has it.

Fifteen call sites were paying for that second read — every route with an :id in it.

The fix is not to thread a cached row through fifteen callers. It is one guard inside the function they all already share: check the cache before you select.

Comment CACHE and I'll send the fix.
